newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy deficit/GDP now at 3.0 pct EMU goal - Prodi.
newsitem.headline: Italy deficit/GDP now at 3.0 pct EMU goal - Prodi.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said Italy's deficit to GDP ratio was now at the 3.0 percent goal required for entry to the single European currency.

Speaking at the Italian Confindustria employers' body annual meeting, he also said he saw the first signs of an economic upturn and that all conditions were in place for a Bank of Italy interest rate cut.

"We have defeated inflation which has fallen from 4.3 percent a year ago to 1.5 percent year-on-year (in May)," Prodi said, confirming forecasts after preliminary Italian cities' May CPI data published on Wednesday.
"As for the deficit/GDP ratio, today we are at 3.0 percent," he said, noting that this was based on public administration criteria used for Maastricht goals.

Prodi said that the lira had appreciated by eight percent since his centre-left coalition took office in May last year, though he did not specify against which currency or basket of currencies he was measuring the rise.

"There are now all the conditions for a reduction in interest rates," he added."Today we are seeing the first signals of an economic recovery. We have attained certain conditions so that this upturn can finally take off."
He said Europe was indispensable to stand up to competition of the global economy. "It is an illusion to imagine that there might be an Italian road to growth outside Europe," he added.

"We are working on a structural revision of welfare state instruments, a reform to eliminate distortions accumulated over decades and to restore a fair and sustainable system, " the Prime Minister said.
Prodi noted that there were some people in the country who were saying that it really would not be too serious if Italy remained outside European economic and monetary union.
"Indeed, some say we should actually opt to stay out of Europe, using the argument of combating unemployment to justify this choice."
He called these ideas "old-fashioned and stale" and belonging to the now out-dated public spending lobby which seemed to be trying to make a come-back.
"Really all they want is for us to renounce Europe to take up again the old practices of public subsidies and investments -- immediate competitivity gains through an exchange rate devaluation.
"A scenario of this kind would in reality have catastrophic consequences for Italy," Prodi said.
